cases.excerpt: We used a nested case-control design to compare the fatty acid compositions in plasma from 120 men who later developed prostate cancer with 120 matched controls who did not.

effect_size.excerpt: For linoleic acid, RRs in successively higher quartiles were 0.7 (95% CI = 0.4-1.5), 0.8 (95% CI = 0.4-1.6), and 0.6 (95% CI = 0.3-1.3), with the lowest quartile as referent (P trend = .24). studies.Reference: Fatty acids and risk of prostate cancer in a nested case-control study in male smokers.
studies.Authors: Männistö S, Pietinen P, Virtanen MJ, Salminen I, Albanes D, Giovannucci E, Virtamo J
studies.Journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology
studies.comparison_type: highest quartile versus lowest quartile among men who received alpha-tocopherol
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Fatty acids of serum cholesterol esters were measured as a percentage of total fatty acids, using capillary gas chromatography.

sample_size.excerpt: One control was selected and matched by age (+/- 1 month) for each case from the cohort subjects alive and free of prostate cancer at the time the case was diagnosed. This study included 198 case-control pairs with baseline serum sample available for both.
sample_size.location: Abstract, sixth sentence; total_n derived from reported group counts 198 + 198 = 396

cases.excerpt: One control was selected and matched by age (+/- 1 month) for each case from the cohort subjects alive and free of prostate cancer at the time the case was diagnosed. This study included 198 case-control pairs with baseline serum sample available for both.

effect_size.excerpt: alpha-Tocopherol supplementation modified the association between serum linoleic acid and prostate cancer risk (P for interaction 0.03); odds ratio was 0.17 (95% confidence interval, 0.04-0.68) in the highest quartile of serum linoleic acid compared with the lowest quartile in men who received alpha-tocopherol, whereas no association was found in men who did not receive alpha-tocopherol.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 5 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.63 (95% CI: 0.45–0.89), suggesting that linoleic acid is associated with a lower risk of prostate cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 60.15%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
